screens.title: KVM Performance Tuning and Optimization
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn how to find and fix the most common performance problems in KVM virtualized environments. We begin by establishing a reliable monitoring baseline using host tools like top, vmstat, iostat and KVM-specific tools such as virt-top. From that baseline, you'll learn focused tuning techniques: C P U pinning and NUMA alignment to reduce scheduling overhead and remote memory latency; huge pages and ballooning to manage VM memory efficiently; and disk input and output options such as virtio-scsi with cache="none" and io="native" for predictable throughput. Each technique includes concrete configuration examples you can apply in VM XML and on the host, and each comes with common pitfalls to avoid, such as over-pinning CPUs or allocating huge pages without persistence. By the end of the chapter you'll be able to collect the right metrics, make one change at a time, and verify the measurable impact. Think of this chapter as a set of focused tools and procedures to keep latency low and throughput high for critical VMs.

Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › KVM Performance
KVM Performance Tuning
Practical host and guest changes that reduce latency and increase throughput

We focus on measurable changes: gather a baseline, make a single targeted change, and re-measure. This reduces risk and makes it easier to identify the true effect of each tuning step.

Common host tools include top, vmstat, iostat and tuned. KVM-specific visibility comes from virt-top and qemu-monitor commands. The chapter shows exact XML and host commands used in enterprise environments.

screens.title: Diagnosing Bottlenecks
screens.narratorSegment: Performance tuning begins with diagnosis. A bottleneck can appear at the C P U, memory, disk, or network layer; the first task is to collect consistent metrics that show which resource is constrained. On the host, tools like top, htop, vmstat and iostat reveal C P U saturation, memory paging, and input and output wait. For KVM-aware views, virt-top displays per-VM C P U, memory and input and output similar to top, and qemu-monitor commands can show block statistics. A concrete example: if iostat shows high await times on the host and virt-top shows a specific guest with high block reads, the problem is disk input and output for that VM. A common misconception is trusting a single metric in isolation; high C P U usage inside a guest might be caused by host-level steal or by frequent page faults due to memory pressure. The right workflow is: collect a baseline, correlate host and guest metrics, and then isolate a single change to test. Key takeaway: diagnosis is about correlation and repeatable measurement, not guesswork. Diagnosing Bottlenecks means always compare host-level metrics with per-vm metrics to identify the true source of a bottleneck.. In practical terms, using host and kvm tools to find where the problem lives. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Correlate host and guest data

content.html:
Core Concept › Diagnosing Bottlenecks
Common Host Commands
top / htop: live CPU and memory per process.
vmstat: system-wide memory, swap and CPU statistics over time.
iostat: block device throughput and latency metrics.
virt-top: per-VM CPU, memory and I/O similar to top.
Example: Interpreting I/O Wait
If iostat shows high await and virt-top shows a single VM with heavy reads, prioritize storage tuning or move the VM to faster storage. If host CPU shows high steal, the host is overloaded by scheduling, not the guest app itself.
Diagnostic Checklist
  • Collect a baseline with the same tools you will use to validate changes.
  • Correlate host metrics with virt-top per-VM stats.
  • Look for spikes in iowait, context switches, or page faults before changing configs.
Key Takeaway

Diagnosis requires both host and guest perspectives; one without the other can mislead your tuning decisions.

screens.title: CPU Pinning
screens.narratorSegment: C P U pinning ties a virtual machine's vCPUs to specific physical C P U cores. This reduces vCPU migration, lowers context switching, and improves cache locality—benefits that matter for latency-sensitive workloads. To implement pinning, modify the VM XML with a static vcpu placement and vcpupin entries that map each vCPU to a physical core. A practical example shows two vCPUs pinned to cores 0 and 1 using a vcpu tag with cpuset and a cputune section specifying vcpupin for each vcpu. A common mistake is pinning to logical hyperthreads without consulting the host C P U topology; this can cause contention if both pins map to the same physical core. Use lscpu -e to inspect C P U, CORE, SOCKET and NODE columns before choosing cpus. After pinning, validate by observing per-core utilization with mpstat and the guest's performance with virt-top. The recommended process is to pin selectively for critical VMs and avoid over-pinning the host, preserving headroom for other guests. CPU Pinning means pin only latency-sensitive vms and verify the physical core mapping with lscpu before committing.. In practical terms, dedicate physical cores to vcpus to reduce jitter and improve cache locality. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Process Flow › CPU Pinning
Pinning Example (XML)
<vcpu placement='static' cpuset='0-1'>2</vcpu>
<cputune>
  <vcpupin vcpu='0' cpuset='0'/>
  <vcpupin vcpu='1' cpuset='1'/>
</cputune>
Run lscpu -e to confirm physical core numbers. After applying, use mpstat -P ALL or htop to ensure pinned vCPU threads run on intended cores and that no unexpected contention appears.
Pinning Checklist
  • Inspect host topology with lscpu -e.
  • Choose physical cores, not just logical IDs.
  • Pin selectively and preserve host capacity.
Common Mistake

Pinning to hyperthreads without checking core layout can leave two vCPUs contending on one physical core. That increases latency, not reduces it.

screens.title: NUMA Awareness
screens.narratorSegment: NUMA stands for Non-Uniform Memory Access. In multi-socket servers, each C P U socket has local memory that it can access faster than memory attached to another socket. For KVM guests, NUMA awareness means allocating a VM's vCPUs and memory from the same NUMA node to avoid remote memory accesses that increase latency. In libvirt XML you can use numatune with memory mode set to strict and a nodeset to pin memory to a node, and combine this with vCPU placement choices so C P U and memory align. A concrete XML fragment shows memory mode='strict' nodeset='0'. A common misconception is trusting automatic allocation on large VMs; automatic placement may cross nodes and cause remote accesses. Use numactl on the host to run processes on specific nodes when testing, and when possible design VM topologies that mirror the physical NUMA layout. The practical insight is: match guest topology to hardware topology to reduce cross-node memory traffic. NUMA Awareness means align vm vcpus and memory with host numa nodes to minimize remote memory latency.. In practical terms, align vcpu and memory to the same numa node for lower latency. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Align VM vCPUs and memory with host NUMA nodes to minimize remote memory latency.

content.html:
Definition › NUMA Awareness
NUMA XML Example
<numatune>
  <memory mode='strict' nodeset='0'/>
  <vcpu placement='auto'/>
</numatune>
If you require explicit CPU pinning to the same node, set vCPU cpuset values that map to that node. Use lscpu and numactl to inspect node mappings and verify behavior under load.
Practical Steps
  1. Inspect NUMA topology: lscpu -e.
  2. Design VM vCPU and memory to fit within a single node when possible.
  3. Set numatune and validate under representative load.
Key Takeaway

Aligning CPU and memory to the same NUMA node reduces latency and improves predictability for multi-socket servers.

screens.title: Huge Pages
screens.narratorSegment: Huge pages are memory pages larger than the standard 4KB, commonly 2MB or 1GB sizes. Using huge pages for VM memory reduces the number of TLB entries the C P U needs to hold and therefore lowers TLB miss overhead—this is particularly beneficial for memory-intensive workloads. The host needs to allocate huge pages first, for example by writing a number into /sys/kernel/mm/hugepages/hugepages-2048kB/nr_hugepages. After allocating, configure the VM's XML memoryBacking to include hugepages. A practical example shows allocating 2048 pages of 2MB for 4GB total and then using in the guest XML. Common mistakes include not making the allocation persistent across reboots or expecting huge pages to be available without sufficient contiguous memory. Always verify allocation and test your workload to confirm reduced TLB miss rates. When used correctly, huge pages deliver measurable reductions in C P U overhead for address translation. Huge Pages means reserve enough contiguous host memory for huge pages and persist the allocation if required for production.. In practical terms, reduce tlb misses by using larger page sizes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition › Huge Pages
Host allocation example
# Allocate 2048 huge pages of 2MB each (total 4GB)
sudo echo 2048 > /sys/kernel/mm/hugepages/hugepages-2048kB/nr_hugepages

# For persistence add vm.nr_hugepages=2048 to /etc/sysctl.conf
After the host allocation, update VM XML memoryBacking to use hugepages so the guest consumes the reserved pages instead of standard pages.
VM XML snippet
<memory unit='KiB'>4194304</memory>
<currentMemory unit='KiB'>4194304</currentMemory>
<memoryBacking>
  <hugepages/>
</memoryBacking>
Verify available huge pages in /proc/meminfo and test the target workload to confirm reduced TLB misses.
Key Takeaway

Huge pages reduce translation overhead for memory-intensive workloads but require host reservation and careful planning to persist across reboots.

screens.title: Memory Ballooning
screens.narratorSegment: Memory ballooning uses a balloon driver inside the guest to allow the hypervisor to reclaim or return memory dynamically. The virtio-balloon driver inflates to force the guest to relinquish memory or deflates to return memory when the host has spare capacity. This enables safe memory over-commitment, but it must be used carefully: if the balloon frequently inflates under load, the guest will suffer performance degradation due to increased page reclamation. The recommended use is for non-critical workloads or as a safety mechanism, not as the primary method for memory management of latency-sensitive services. The VM XML shows how to set a larger maximum memory and a lower currentMemory so the balloon can manage the rest. Always monitor guest-level swap and page fault rates to detect excessive ballooning effects before production deployment. Memory Ballooning means ballooning is useful for over-commitment but avoid for critical vms that require stable memory residency.. In practical terms, dynamically reclaim or return memory between host and guest. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition › Memory Ballooning
XML: Balloon with adjustable currentMemory
<memory unit='KiB'>4194304</memory>
<currentMemory unit='KiB'>2097152</currentMemory>
<devices>
  <memballoon model='virtio'></memballoon>
</devices>
Here the VM has a max of 4GB but starts at 2GB; the balloon driver lets the host manage the remaining pages dynamically.
When to avoid ballooning
  • Latency-sensitive databases that require stable memory allocations.
  • Workloads that swap heavily when memory is reclaimed, which increases I/O.
Key Takeaway

Use ballooning as a controlled tool for overcommitment and monitor guest swap and page faults to avoid performance degradation.

screens.title: Disk I/O Options
screens.narratorSegment: Disk input and output tuning balances throughput, latency, and data durability. The chapter highlights virtio-scsi as the preferred driver for performance and features over virtio-blk or emulated controllers. In VM XML, disk driver options cache='none' and io='native' enable direct input and output and bypass host page cache and some QEMU buffering, which can produce more predictable performance for input and output-intensive workloads. However, bypassing caches increases the risk of data loss on host power failure if guests don't flush disk buffers frequently. A concrete XML disk example includes driver name='qemu' type='qcow2' cache='none' io='native' and a virtio target. Storage backend selection is equally important: choose fast local SSDs, dedicated LVM volumes, or performant shared storage for critical VMs rather than slow NFS. Finally, tune the host input and output scheduler to mq-deadline or noop for SSD workloads. Always test under realistic load to validate the trade-offs. Disk I/O Options means cache='none' with io='native' improves predictability but requires careful attention to guest flush behavior and backups.. In practical terms, choose drivers and i/o settings for predictable throughput and durability. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Lab Steps (condensed)

screens.title: Safe Tuning Methodology
screens.narratorSegment: A repeatable methodology keeps tuning safe and auditable. Start with a baseline that captures representative workload behavior. When you change a parameter, make only one change at a time so you can attribute any difference in performance to that change. Use the same monitoring tools for baseline and validation to ensure comparisons are meaningful. Document the time window, tools, and workloads used for each test. A common mistake is to apply multiple changes at once and then assume observed improvements came from the most visible change; this makes rollbacks risky. For production systems, stage changes in a test environment that mirrors the production topology, and schedule maintenance windows when necessary. Finally, always include recovery steps and a rollback plan before making potentially disruptive host-level changes such as huge page allocations that reduce available memory for other guests. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn how to find and fix the most common performance problems in KVM virtualized environments. We begin by establishing a reliable monitoring baseline using host tools like top, vmstat, iostat and KVM-specific tools such as virt-top. From that baseline, you'll learn focused tuning techniques: C P U pinning and NUMA alignment to reduce scheduling overhead and remote memory latency; huge pages and ballooning to manage VM memory efficiently; and disk input and output options such as virtio-scsi with cache="none" and io="native" for predictable throughput. Each technique includes concrete configuration examples you can apply in VM XML and on the host, and each comes with common pitfalls to avoid, such as over-pinning CPUs or allocating huge pages without persistence. By the end of the chapter you'll be able to collect the right metrics, make one change at a time, and verify the measurable impact. Think of this chapter as a set of focused tools and procedures to keep latency low and throughput high for critical VMs.

These objectives focus your work on measurement, targeted configuration, and verification. You will learn how to identify C P U, memory, disk, and network bottlenecks using host and KVM tools, and how to prioritize which resource to tune first. You will practice concrete VM-level changes such as C P U pinning and NUMA alignment to reduce latency and improve cache locality. Memory techniques include configuring huge pages to reduce translation overhead and using ballooning carefully when over-committing. Finally, you'll apply disk tuning choices like virtio-scsi with direct input and output and understand the safety trade-offs. Each objective maps to a measurable milestone: collect baseline metrics, apply an isolated change, and confirm improvement with the same monitoring tools. This makes tuning repeatable and safe for production systems. Learning Objectives means every tuning step should be validated against a baseline using the same metrics.. In practical terms, what you will be able to do after this chapter. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

These additional objectives emphasize operational skills and tool use for ongoing performance management. You will learn to use virt-top and qemu-monitor commands to observe VM-level C P U, memory, and block statistics in real time, and how to interpret those metrics in the context of host-level tools. You'll also practice storage and scheduler tuning on the host, choosing appropriate input and output schedulers for SSDs or spinning disks. Finally, we stress a methodical approach: develop a baseline, make a single change, and re-evaluate to avoid introducing instability. This discipline is what makes tuning safe in production environments and ensures changes have a traceable benefit. Learning Objectives (cont.) means using the same tools for baseline and validation makes tuning outcomes reliable and repeatable.. In practical terms, secondary skills and monitoring practices. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. Performance tuning begins with diagnosis. A bottleneck can appear at the C P U, memory, disk, or network layer; the first task is to collect consistent metrics that show which resource is constrained. On the host, tools like top, htop, vmstat and iostat reveal C P U saturation, memory paging, and input and output wait. For KVM-aware views, virt-top displays per-VM C P U, memory and input and output similar to top, and qemu-monitor commands can show block statistics. A concrete example: if iostat shows high await times on the host and virt-top shows a specific guest with high block reads, the problem is disk input and output for that VM. A common misconception is trusting a single metric in isolation; high C P U usage inside a guest might be caused by host-level steal or by frequent page faults due to memory pressure. The right workflow is: collect a baseline, correlate host and guest metrics, and then isolate a single change to test. Key takeaway: diagnosis is about correlation and repeatable measurement, not guesswork. Diagnosing Bottlenecks means always compare host-level metrics with per-vm metrics to identify the true source of a bottleneck.. In practical terms, using host and kvm tools to find where the problem lives. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

C P U pinning ties a virtual machine's vCPUs to specific physical C P U cores. This reduces vCPU migration, lowers context switching, and improves cache locality—benefits that matter for latency-sensitive workloads. To implement pinning, modify the VM XML with a static vcpu placement and vcpupin entries that map each vCPU to a physical core. A practical example shows two vCPUs pinned to cores 0 and 1 using a vcpu tag with cpuset and a cputune section specifying vcpupin for each vcpu. A common mistake is pinning to logical hyperthreads without consulting the host C P U topology; this can cause contention if both pins map to the same physical core. Use lscpu -e to inspect C P U, CORE, SOCKET and NODE columns before choosing cpus. After pinning, validate by observing per-core utilization with mpstat and the guest's performance with virt-top. The recommended process is to pin selectively for critical VMs and avoid over-pinning the host, preserving headroom for other guests. CPU Pinning means pin only latency-sensitive vms and verify the physical core mapping with lscpu before committing.. In practical terms, dedicate physical cores to vcpus to reduce jitter and improve cache locality. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

NUMA stands for Non-Uniform Memory Access. In multi-socket servers, each C P U socket has local memory that it can access faster than memory attached to another socket. For KVM guests, NUMA awareness means allocating a VM's vCPUs and memory from the same NUMA node to avoid remote memory accesses that increase latency. In libvirt XML you can use numatune with memory mode set to strict and a nodeset to pin memory to a node, and combine this with vCPU placement choices so C P U and memory align. A concrete XML fragment shows memory mode='strict' nodeset='0'. A common misconception is trusting automatic allocation on large VMs; automatic placement may cross nodes and cause remote accesses. Use numactl on the host to run processes on specific nodes when testing, and when possible design VM topologies that mirror the physical NUMA layout. The practical insight is: match guest topology to hardware topology to reduce cross-node memory traffic. NUMA Awareness means align vm vcpus and memory with host numa nodes to minimize remote memory latency.. In practical terms, align vcpu and memory to the same numa node for lower latency. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Huge pages are memory pages larger than the standard 4KB, commonly 2MB or 1GB sizes. Using huge pages for VM memory reduces the number of TLB entries the C P U needs to hold and therefore lowers TLB miss overhead—this is particularly beneficial for memory-intensive workloads. The host needs to allocate huge pages first, for example by writing a number into /sys/kernel/mm/hugepages/hugepages-2048kB/nr_hugepages. After allocating, configure the VM's XML memoryBacking to include hugepages. A practical example shows allocating 2048 pages of 2MB for 4GB total and then using in the guest XML. Common mistakes include not making the allocation persistent across reboots or expecting huge pages to be available without sufficient contiguous memory. Always verify allocation and test your workload to confirm reduced TLB miss rates. When used correctly, huge pages deliver measurable reductions in C P U overhead for address translation. Huge Pages means reserve enough contiguous host memory for huge pages and persist the allocation if required for production.. In practical terms, reduce tlb misses by using larger page sizes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. Memory ballooning uses a balloon driver inside the guest to allow the hypervisor to reclaim or return memory dynamically. The virtio-balloon driver inflates to force the guest to relinquish memory or deflates to return memory when the host has spare capacity.
